title: Graph Neural Networks for Accurate Quasiparticle Energy Levels in Large Supercells of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
authors: Rafael R. Del Grande, David A. Strubbe
abstract: The GW method is the one of the main workhorses of the materials science community to accurately calculate the electronic bandgap of materials, as it overcomes the gap underestimation problem from Density Functional Theory (DFT). Despite its accuracy, its computational cost becomes prohibitive when calculations have more than 10-100 atoms, which makes more difficult its use for defects, surfaces and moiré systems that demand large supercells. To overcome this problem, we developed a Graph Neural Network trained with smaller GW calculations which can make accurate predictions on large supercells at a small fraction of the computational cost. Our model uses as features the projection of DFT wavefunctions into localized atomic orbitals, while graph nodes represent the atomic positions and edges represent atom to atom distances, which captures the system geometry. We explore how to do "small AI", providing a workflow of how to create a personal and convenient dataset of GW calculations to train the model that can be applied to different materials so that the final user does not need to rely on massive datasets. We define what must be included in the training dataset to capture the physics of our objective simulation, and perform a Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters. In the case of monolayer MoS$_2$ with a sulfur vacancy our GNN models achieve high accuracy (MAE ranging 10 to 50 meV) with a simplified workflow applicable to other materials, accelerating accurate large electronic structure calculations.

infographic.key_insight: A graph neural network trained on smaller GW calculations predicts quasiparticle energy levels in large supercells at a fraction of the computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make accurate electronic-structure modeling more practical for defects, surfaces, and moiré systems where direct GW calculations become prohibitively expensive.
method: Represent atoms as graph nodes and encode interatomic distances on edges.
Use DFT wavefunction projections onto localized atomic orbitals as model features.
Build a targeted, compact GW training dataset and tune hyperparameters with Bayesian optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: For monolayer MoS₂ with a sulfur vacancy, the abstract reports mean absolute errors of 10–50 meV.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy beyond the demonstrated defect system remains to be established, and training data must capture the physics of the target simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Graph Neural Networks for Accurate Quasiparticle Energy Levels in Large Supercells of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides

title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
authors: Yingheng Wang, Francesco Ricci, Zhilong Wang, Tao Yu, Junwen Bai, Xiangyun Lei
abstract: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: DeepDOSReasoner predicts electronic and phonon densities of states while enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Millisecond spectral predictions enable high-throughput screening for electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic materials properties.
method: Decode spectra from crystal structures using atom-to-energy source attention.
Refine normalized spectra through learned continuity-equation transport.
Recover element-resolved spectral contributions without supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports best accuracy across all evaluated eDOS and phDOS metrics, plus new DFT validation on 8,106 uncharted materials confirming VB gaps in 25 of the model’s top 50 candidates.
infographic.watch_item: Physical constraints do not guarantee accurate spectra for every material; high-priority candidates still warrant DFT or experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery

title: Strain-Induced Tetragonal-to-Cubic Transition in MAPbI$_3$ from Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics
authors: Daan Holleman, Luuk Klein Nagelvoort, Monica Morales-Masis, Linn Leppert
abstract: Metal-halide perovskites are promising photovoltaic absorbers whose optoelectronic properties are highly tunable. Epitaxial strain offers a route to stabilize desirable phases, tune band gaps, and reduce energetic disorder, but rational strain engineering requires predictive models. Static, zero-temperature "strained-bulk" density functional theory (DFT) calculations, successful for oxide perovskites, neglect the dynamic disorder and anharmonicity that govern halide perovskites at ambient temperature. Here, we show that molecular dynamics (MD) based on machine-learned force fields trained on-the-fly on DFT reproduces the structural and optoelectronic response of methylammonium (MA) lead iodide (MAPbI$_3$) to epitaxial strain at 300 K. We simulate bulk and free-standing slab models across experimentally accessible biaxial strains by locking the in-plane lattice vectors in nanosecond-long simulations. We predict a tetragonal-to-cubic transition at $\sim$0.5% tensile strain, marked by $c/a = 1$ and the loss of the $a^0a^0c^-$ tilting pattern, in agreement with experiments on epitaxial MAPbI$_3$ films on KCl. MA cations retain preferential orientations in the strain-induced cubic phase, unlike in its temperature-induced counterpart. Bulk and slab models yield consistent trends, with surface effects decaying within a few octahedral layers. Band gaps computed as ensemble averages over MD snapshots blue-shift under tensile strain, consistent with experiment, whereas static calculations on averaged structures predict a red shift. Our study positions MD with constrained lattice vectors as a method for predicting finite-temperature strain phase diagrams and guiding the epitaxial design of perovskite absorbers.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learned molecular dynamics predicts that approximately 0.5% biaxial tensile strain drives MAPbI₃ from tetragonal to cubic at 300 K while retaining preferential molecular orientations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Finite-temperature strain modeling can guide epitaxial phase stabilization and band-gap tuning in perovskite photovoltaic absorbers.
method: Train machine-learned force fields on-the-fly using DFT.
Run nanosecond bulk and free-standing slab simulations with fixed in-plane lattice vectors.
Track lattice symmetry, octahedral tilts, and band gaps averaged over MD snapshots.
infographic.evidence_signal: The predicted transition agrees with experiments on MAPbI₃ films on KCl, and ensemble-averaged band gaps reproduce the experimental tensile-strain blue shift that static averaged-structure calculations miss.
infographic.watch_item: Free-standing slabs do not explicitly capture substrate-interface chemistry, which may affect transfer to specific epitaxial systems.
infographic.paper_title: Strain-Induced Tetragonal-to-Cubic Transition in MAPbI$_3$ from Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics

title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction
authors: Changzhi Ai, Frank Abild-Pedersen, Johannes Voss
abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme). Here, we present AdsNet, an equivariant graph neural network that directly predicts adsorption energies in a single forward pass, which operates on a local graph restricted only to adsorbate atoms and its immediate surface neighbors within a cutoff radius. This local graph formulation decouples computational complexity from total system size while encoding continuous geometric features (interatomic distances and directional vectors) enabling sensitivity to subtle variations in local bonding environments. AdsNet adopts a message-passing architecture with scalar and vector node features over multiple interaction layers. Trained on AdsTraj, a dataset of 33,920 density functional theory (DFT) calculated structures spanning 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates (H*, C*, O*, CO*, OH*, HOCO*), the model achieves an adsorption energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.032 eV and a force RMSE of 0.047 eV/A. Analytic forces obtained via automatic differentiation enable structure relaxation through a projected gradient descent algorithm with adaptive line search, eliminating entire geometry optimizations. Additionally, AdsNet uniquely decomposes predicted adsorption energies into contributions from individual atoms within the local adsorbate graph - an interpretability feature unattainable with conventional machine-learning potentials. AdsNet thus establishes an accurate, highly efficient, and interpretable framework for large-scale adsorption energy prediction and local interface relaxation across various material surfaces.

infographic.key_insight: AdsNet predicts adsorption energies in one forward pass using an equivariant graph neural network focused on the adsorbate and nearby surface atoms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its local representation supports efficient catalyst screening and local interface relaxation without processing the full atomic system.
method: Build a cutoff-based local graph containing adsorbate atoms and nearby surface neighbors.
Use scalar–vector message passing to encode interatomic distances and directions and predict atom-resolved energy contributions.
Obtain analytic forces by automatic differentiation for projected gradient descent relaxation with adaptive line search.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on AdsTraj’s 33,920 DFT structures spanning 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates, AdsNet reports energy RMSE of 0.032 eV and force RMSE of 0.047 eV/Å.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalization beyond the reported metals and adsorbates; a local cutoff may also miss relevant longer-range interactions.
infographic.paper_title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction

title: Lattice Thermal Conductivity of MgO and the MgSiO$_3$ Polymorphs Bridgmanite and Post-Perovskite at Lower-Mantle Conditions Using Fine-Tuned MACE Potentials
authors: Amrendra Kumar Tiwari, Sandro Jahn
abstract: Heat flow across the core-mantle boundary (CMB) depends on the lattice thermal conductivity ($κ_{\mathrm{latt}}$) of lowermost-mantle minerals, yet calculated CMB values for MgO differ severalfold, and high-temperature estimates of the conductivity increase across the bridgmanite-post-perovskite transition range from about 20 to 50%. Direct solutions of the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation (LBTE) require thousands of density functional theory (DFT) force evaluations per thermodynamic state. Here we replace these evaluations with phase-specific, fine-tuned MACE potentials for MgO, MgSiO3 bridgmanite (Pv), and MgSiO3 post-perovskite (PPv). The potentials reproduce DFT energies, forces, stresses, pressure-volume relations, and compressed-state phonons for all three phases. For MgO at 0 GPa, replacing MACE forces with DFT forces in otherwise identical transport calculations changes $κ_{\mathrm{latt}}$ by 0.2% at 300 K and 1.9% at 2000 K. PPv is 44-55% more conductive than Pv at the same pressure and temperature and strongly anisotropic, with $κ_{[100]}/κ_{[010]}$ ranging from 1.7 to 2.1. The quasi-harmonic phase boundary has a Clapeyron slope of $(7.4 \pm 0.1)$ MPa/K and intersects a model geotherm at 116.2 GPa and 2660 K, where the transition raises the silicate conductivity by 47%, to 8.6 W/(m K). Heating in the basal thermal boundary layer lowers the MgO and PPv conductivities to 37.3 and 6.7 W/(m K) at the CMB, where Hashin-Shtrikman bounds of 9.5-11.4 W/(m K) for an Fe-free aggregate of 80 vol% silicate and 20 vol% MgO encompass the 10 W/(m K) used in earlier heat-flow estimates. The density-temperature parameterizations provide an intrinsic end-member reference for lower-mantle thermal models.

infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuned MACE potentials predict that post-perovskite conducts lattice heat 44–55% better than bridgmanite at matched lower-mantle conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The resulting conductivity parameterizations support lower-mantle thermal models, with Fe-free aggregate estimates of 9.5–11.4 W/(m K) at the core–mantle boundary.
method: Fine-tune phase-specific MACE potentials for MgO, bridgmanite, and post-perovskite.
Replace DFT force evaluations in linearized phonon Boltzmann transport calculations.
Combine quasi-harmonic phase-boundary calculations with aggregate conductivity bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: For MgO at 0 GPa, otherwise identical transport calculations using MACE versus DFT forces differ in lattice conductivity by 0.2% at 300 K and 1.9% at 2000 K.
infographic.watch_item: These intrinsic, Fe-free end-member estimates are a reference rather than a complete conductivity model for chemically complex mantle material.
infographic.paper_title: Lattice Thermal Conductivity of MgO and the MgSiO$_3$ Polymorphs Bridgmanite and Post-Perovskite at Lower-Mantle Conditions Using Fine-Tuned MACE Potentials

title: Photocatalytic Water Splitting in GeC/ReS$_2$ van der Waals Heterostructures
authors: Parisa Beyranvand, Ismaeil Abdolhosseini Sarsari, Noejung Park
abstract: Photocatalytic water splitting is considered as one of the most promising approaches for the green hydrogen production. But the rapid recombination of photogenerated electron-hole pairs severely inhibits its photocatalytic efficiency. Construction of van der Waals heterostructures is a good way to suppress this recombination. However, in staggered band heterostructures, the charge transfer could occur either through the type-II or the direct Z-scheme mechanism. Therefore it is very important to identify which mechanism is dominant. In the present work, we systematically study the GeC/ReS$_2$ heterostructure using first-principles density functional theory (DFT). The system exhibits good thermodynamic, dynamic and thermal stability and an indirect band gap of 1.38 eV which greatly enhances the visible-light absorption. We find that the direct Z-scheme mechanism is the dominant interfacial charge transfer by analysing band alignment and Gibbs free energy pathways. The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) can be driven spontaneously in the pH range $4 \le \text{pH} \le 14$ under light irradiation for both type-II and Z-scheme pathways but the energy barrier is much lower for the Z-scheme mechanism. Moreover, the type-II mechanism is not suitable for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but the Z-scheme mechanism can promote HER well in the entire pH range ($0 \le \text{pH} \le 14$). Remarkably, the strain-free (pristine) condition exhibits a solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency of 41.40\%, well above the 10\% threshold for commercial viability. The STH efficiency is further enhanced to 60.68\% under a tensile strain of +6\%. To summarise, the Z-scheme strain-tunable GeC/ReS$_2$ heterostructure is a promising and efficient photocatalyst for overall water splitting.

infographic.key_insight: DFT predicts that GeC/ReS₂ favors direct Z-scheme charge transfer, retaining the redox power needed for photocatalytic overall water splitting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tensile strain offers a route to tune this candidate hydrogen-production photocatalyst, with predicted solar-to-hydrogen efficiency rising from 41.40% to 60.68% at +6% strain.
method: First-principles DFT analysis of stability and electronic structure.
Band-alignment and Gibbs free-energy comparisons of type-II and direct Z-scheme pathways.
Evaluation of pH-dependent reaction energetics and strain-dependent efficiency.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations indicate an indirect 1.38 eV band gap, favorable Z-scheme HER energetics across pH 0–14, and light-driven OER across pH 4–14.
infographic.watch_item: The efficiencies and dominant charge-transfer mechanism are computational predictions requiring experimental validation, including practical control of +6% tensile strain.
infographic.paper_title: Photocatalytic Water Splitting in GeC/ReS$_2$ van der Waals Heterostructures

title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys
authors: Xiang Meng, Shuhei Shinzato, Zhiqiang Zhao, Linfeng Yu, Jian Guo, Liangli Chu
abstract: Boron (B) microalloying can effectively refine microstructures of as-cast TiAl alloys and regulate their mechanical properties. Yet, how dilute B exists in TiAl and interacts with defects and how these interactions govern high-temperature deformation remain elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate defect-mediated B redistribution in TiAl alloys and its consequences for their deformation using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations augmented with a newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning potential. As a typical product of B microalloying, borides are markedly stiffer than the TiAl matrix and act as brittle reinforcing phases, while borides/matrix interfacial adhesion depends on surface termination and stacking sequence. In the bulk, interstitial B tends to be trapped at Ti-rich octahedral sites by high migration barriers but can kinetically evolve into substitutional dopants upon approaching Al vacancies. Increased tensile stress and vacancy concentration further promote B enrichment in the bulk. B is enriched at semi-coherent $γ/α_2$ boundaries and preferentially partitions into the $α_2$ phase. In polycrystalline TiAl, B accumulates primarily in disordered regions, raising the average flow stress by 9.4% at 1 at.% B and 900 K. This strengthening is accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation. Simulated microstructural evolution and stacking-fault energetics indicate that B impedes dislocation glide via local pinning and suppresses deformation twinning, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation. By linking solute redistribution to defect interactions and deformation, these findings establish an atomistic framework for understanding and designing high-performance alloys based on interstitial solutes.

infographic.key_insight: Boron redistributes toward defects in TiAl and strengthens the alloy by locally pinning dislocations and suppressing deformation twinning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling boron content and defect populations could help design TiAl alloys with greater resistance to high-temperature plastic deformation.
method: Hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations.
New high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential.
Atomistic analysis of boron partitioning, defect interactions, and deformation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulated polycrystalline TiAl at 900 K, 1 at.% boron increased average flow stress by 9.4% and reduced shear strain accumulation.
infographic.watch_item: The strengthening result is simulation-based; experimental validation is needed, and stiff, brittle borides introduce a potential mechanical trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys

title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
authors: Harry Sevi, Joonatan E. M. Laulainen
abstract: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

infographic.key_insight: Better reliability diagnostics do not necessarily improve materials screening or reduce DFT verification costs at a required recall.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate reliability tools by the DFT they help avoid while retaining near-hull candidates, rather than by diagnostic accuracy alone.
method: Rank candidate crystals with MACE-MP, CHGNet, and Orb V3 before DFT verification.
Test novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits against a recall-constrained screening objective.
Use two oracle analyses to distinguish misaligned reliability targets from finite-budget audit limitations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all three interventions, improvements in their immediate diagnostic targets did not reliably translate into better downstream screening decisions.
infographic.watch_item: Audit-guided model routing depends on both decision-aligned targets and sufficient audit information; sparse audits did not yield robust benefits in the evaluated settings.
infographic.paper_title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery

title: Native vacancy energetics and association in TiN and CrN: chemical potential dependence, clustering, and surface effects
authors: Barsha Bhattacharjee, Emilia Olsson
abstract: Native vacancy populations in transition-metal nitride coatings reflect vacancy formation, association, and depth-dependent stability. Using density functional theory (DFT), we compare these effects in rocksalt TiN and CrN in bulk and at (001) surfaces, within phase-stability-constrained chemical potential ranges. In TiN, $V_\mathrm{N}$ is favoured under N-poor and $V_\mathrm{Ti}$ under N-rich conditions; in CrN, $V_\mathrm{N}$ remains preferred throughout its stability range. Association energies are referenced to corresponding isolated vacancies where positive values mean association lowers the energy and negative values favour separation. Mean bulk association energies for mixed metal-nitrogen pairs are $+0.132$ eV in TiN and $+1.053$ eV in CrN. At (001) surfaces, $V_\mathrm{N}$ in TiN prefers the surface and $V_\mathrm{Ti}$ the first subsurface layer. In CrN, $V_\mathrm{N}$ has similar formation energies at the surface and first subsurface layer, with a slight preference for the latter; $V_\mathrm{Cr}$ slightly prefers the second subsurface layer. Surface cluster energies are referenced to separated vacancies at their preferred depths. The compact $2V_\mathrm{Ti}+2V_\mathrm{N}$ cluster in TiN has favourable association in bulk ($+0.217$ eV per vacancy) but unfavourable association at the surface ($-0.346$ eV per vacancy). By contrast, $2V_\mathrm{Cr}+2V_\mathrm{N}$ in CrN remains stabilised, with its association energy decreasing from $+1.188$ to $+0.431$ eV per vacancy. CrN's stronger association occurs without larger structural distortions and is accompanied by distinct Cr-centred magnetic responses.

infographic.key_insight: DFT predicts stronger vacancy association in CrN than TiN, with compact mixed-vacancy clusters remaining stabilised at CrN(001) surfaces but becoming unfavourable at TiN(001) surfaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for nitrogen availability and vacancy depth could help guide defect control in TiN and CrN coatings.
method: DFT calculations of native vacancies in bulk rocksalt TiN and CrN and at (001) surfaces.
Formation energies evaluated across phase-stability-constrained chemical potentials.
Association energies referenced to isolated vacancies, using preferred depths for surface comparisons.
infographic.evidence_signal: For compact clusters containing two metal and two nitrogen vacancies, association energies change from +0.217 to −0.346 eV per vacancy in TiN and from +1.188 to +0.431 eV per vacancy in CrN between bulk and surface; positive values indicate favourable association.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports DFT energetics, not experimental validation or vacancy migration kinetics, so practical clustering rates remain unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Native vacancy energetics and association in TiN and CrN: chemical potential dependence, clustering, and surface effects

title: A macroscopic-atom spectral theory of grain-boundary segregation in multicomponent alloys
authors: Dennis Boakye, Chuang Deng
abstract: Predicting grain-boundary segregation in multicomponent alloys remains challenging because existing spectral approaches require alloy-specific atomistic calculations to resolve segregation-energy distributions and correlations across non-equivalent boundary sites. Here, we develop a transferable macroscopic-atom spectral theory that predicts the joint segregation behavior of multiple species from physically interpretable elemental descriptors. The theory is founded on the finding that local strain and bond deficit account for 91\% of the site-to-site co-variation of 40 solutes in a density-functional-theory (DFT) Al polycrystal. Linked to atomic size and surface enthalpy, these coordinates allow prediction of individual segregation spectra and their cross-species correlations, which determine whether species compete for or share grain-boundary sites. A closed-system formulation unifies host-element redistribution and dilute-solute segregation, couples metallic and light-element sublattices, and accounts for bulk compound formation and solute pairing. Calibrated using binary spectra only, the theory predicts unseen-host spectral means with a correlation coefficient of 0.81, outperforms embedded-atom spectra against DFT benchmarks, and ranks site competition across 870 solute pairs with a Spearman coefficient of 0.90. Without fitting to multicomponent observations, it reproduces 11 of 12 equilibrium Fe ternaries and 49 of 55 Mg ternaries. Predictions recorded before simulations of an 82,699-atom polycrystal identify site competition as the baseline behavior and metal-metalloid pair chemistry as a source of deviations requiring atomistic resolution. These results establish a physically grounded route to screening grain-boundary chemistry in multicomponent alloys, including steels and high-entropy alloys.

infographic.key_insight: A transferable, physics-based spectral theory predicts which alloying elements compete for or share grain-boundary sites using elemental descriptors rather than alloy-specific atomistic calculations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate grain-boundary chemistry screening for multicomponent alloys, including steels and high-entropy alloys.
method: Represent segregation spectra through local strain and bond deficit, linked to atomic size and surface enthalpy.
Predict cross-species spectral correlations to distinguish site competition from site sharing.
Use a closed-system model incorporating host redistribution, coupled sublattices, compound formation, and solute pairing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calibrated only on binary spectra, the theory achieved unseen-host mean correlation r = 0.81, ranked competition across 870 solute pairs with Spearman ρ = 0.90, and reproduced 11/12 Fe and 49/55 Mg equilibrium ternaries without multicomponent fitting.
infographic.watch_item: Metal–metalloid pair chemistry can cause deviations from baseline site competition that still require atomistic resolution.
infographic.paper_title: A macroscopic-atom spectral theory of grain-boundary segregation in multicomponent alloys

title: Mixing and Preserving Properties of Non-van der Waals 2D Materials in Sandwich-like Heterostructures
authors: Anastasiia Nihei, Rico Friedrich
abstract: Heterostructure interfaces created by stacking two-dimensional (2D) materials outline an appealing route towards achieving advanced electronic and magnetic functionalities at the nanoscale. Non-van der Waals (non-vdW) sandwich-like heterostructures (HSs) are build out of non-vdW 2D materials derived from non-layered crystals and establish a new frontier enabling strong interfacial coupling. Employing ab initio density functional theory (DFT), we investigate two classes of such trilayer HSs: purely non-vdW assemblies and hybrid vdW/non-vdW/vdW stacks. We show that non-vdW sandwiches undergo pronounced geometric reconstruction forming chemically bonded interfaces with large absolute binding energies up to an order of magnitude larger than those of conventional vdW HSs. These strong interactions drive extensive electronic hybridization, band gap renormalization, and tunable interlayer magnetic coupling. In contrast, vdW encapsulation largely protects the intrinsic atomic and electronic structure of the non-vdW sheet from the environment , while enabling charge transfer doping of the vdW layers. Our results thus establish sandwich HSs a versatile interface design platform, spanning interaction regimes from weakly perturbed encapsulation to strongly interacting chemically bonded systems with emergent electronic and magnetic behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Sandwich heterostructures can either strongly reshape non-van der Waals 2D materials through chemical bonding or largely preserve them through van der Waals encapsulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Interface selection offers a route to tuning nanoscale electronic and magnetic behavior while choosing between strong coupling and structural protection.
method: Use ab initio density functional theory.
Compare purely non-vdW trilayers with hybrid vdW/non-vdW/vdW stacks.
Analyze reconstruction, binding, electronic structure, and magnetic coupling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The calculations indicate absolute binding energies up to an order of magnitude larger than conventional vdW heterostructures, alongside electronic hybridization, band-gap changes, and tunable interlayer magnetic coupling.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational predictions but does not establish experimental synthesis feasibility or device-level performance.
infographic.paper_title: Mixing and Preserving Properties of Non-van der Waals 2D Materials in Sandwich-like Heterostructures

title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
authors: Yanlin Fei, Lei Li, Shaolong Chen, Nazhou Liu, Xinmiao Yu, Madalina Ciobanu
abstract: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.

infographic.key_insight: MatHarness supports open-ended computational materials research from ideation to manuscript writing by combining robust execution, adaptive scientific reasoning, and multi-agent review.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework demonstrates how AI agents can sustain multi-week simulation campaigns while recovering from failures and retaining targeted human oversight.
method: Pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing improve execution robustness.
Persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model support plan revision.
A heterogeneous multi-agent round table coordinates research under human approval and strategic steering.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a multi-week Cu–Zn segregation study using roughly 1,000 GPU-hours, 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations prescreened 50 production DFT relaxations; the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and an independent auditor overturned one over-attributed claim.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence comes from one research campaign, and its materials conclusions are restricted to sampled metallic dilute-limit models with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions.
infographic.paper_title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science

title: DED-Agent: An agentic AI method for autonomous thermal simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition
authors: Michael Song, Yilong Dai, Lin Cheng
abstract: In metal additive manufacturing (AM), process parameters set the local thermal history, which governs defects, microstructure and properties. Laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, scan strategy and position combine into a design space of 10^4-10^6 conditions, which is beyond what human experts can map by hand with finite element (FE) thermal models: every model must be set up, meshed, solved and calibrated by an expert, and calibrating unknown heat-source parameters alone can take days to weeks. This paper presents DED-Agent, an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) method for autonomous simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition (L-DED). A supervisor agent coordinates three specialist agents that share a structured simulation specification and call open-source tools. An intent agent turns a plain-language request into a validated specification, a simulation agent builds, runs and checks an FE thermal model through physics-aware step-by-step reasoning, and a calibration agent identifies key heat-source parameters against experimental data (e.g., thermocouple data) using a high-order proper generalized decomposition (HOPGD) surrogate within a trust-region search. On five benchmark builds, from single-track walls to a multi-track band on a cylindrical tube, the agents built executable thermal models without manual intervention, with 4.1-9.1% error for the simple and medium builds. Within three calibration rounds, the error fell to 0.9-2.5%. The surrogate matched full FE to within 0.08-1.55% and shortened calibration by 5-13 times. Agentic AI can thus autonomously establish reliable, accurate simulation models for AM processes and accelerate the search for process parameters that control microstructure.

infographic.key_insight: DED-Agent autonomously builds and calibrates laser directed energy deposition thermal models, reducing reported error to 0.9–2.5% within three calibration rounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster thermal model development could help engineers explore process parameters that influence defects, microstructure and properties.
method: A supervisor coordinates intent, simulation and calibration agents through a shared structured specification.
Agents translate plain-language requests into validated specifications and build, run and check finite element thermal models.
A high-order proper generalized decomposition surrogate accelerates trust-region calibration of heat-source parameters against experimental data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five benchmark builds, executable models were generated without manual intervention; surrogate predictions differed from full finite element results by 0.08–1.55%, with calibration accelerated 5–13×.
infographic.watch_item: Validation covers five benchmark builds; broader reliability and direct microstructure prediction are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: DED-Agent: An agentic AI method for autonomous thermal simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition

title: Thermodynamics of complex crystals from a generalized mean-field bond model
authors: Raynol Dsouza, Thomas D. Swinburne, Jörg Neugebauer
abstract: We extend our previously introduced mean-field bond model from unary fcc lattices to crystals with multiple chemical species and sublattices, accurately predicting finite-temperature thermodynamics without statistical sampling. Our generalization reformulates the model in terms of the Wyckoff positions of the crystal, representing each by one atom, and solving for the bond density of the reference bond of each of its neighbor shells. Bond-bond correlation functions are built from the zero-temperature force constants, allowing the deviation of every bond in the crystal to be expressed through linear functions of the reference bond of a shell. Thermodynamic self-consistency is enforced by requiring a single virial temperature for the whole crystal, and compatibility of average bond lengths with crystal volume. Model predictions are validated against molecular dynamics simulations of unary, binary, and ternary crystals using Morse-type bonding potentials, parametrized for each shell from the force constants of empirical interatomic potentials at several isotropic strains. In each case, the predicted bond densities and thermodynamics agree with the simulations to within their statistical uncertainty. We discuss strategies for combining the model with bonding potentials parametrized from first principles and foundation models to predict the finite-temperature thermodynamics of complex crystals at ab initio accuracy without statistical sampling.

infographic.key_insight: A generalized mean-field bond model predicts finite-temperature thermodynamics of multispecies, multisublattice crystals without statistical sampling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a route to thermodynamic predictions for complex crystalline materials without sampling-intensive molecular dynamics.
method: Represent each Wyckoff position by one atom and solve reference-bond densities for its neighbor shells.
Use zero-temperature force constants to construct bond–bond correlations.
Enforce a common virial temperature and compatibility between average bond lengths and crystal volume.
infographic.evidence_signal: For unary, binary, and ternary crystals with shell-specific Morse-type potentials, predicted bond densities and thermodynamics agree with molecular dynamics within statistical uncertainty.
infographic.watch_item: Ab initio accuracy remains a proposed extension; validation here uses Morse-type potentials parametrized from empirical-potential force constants.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamics of complex crystals from a generalized mean-field bond model

title: Accelerating interatomic potential development through student-driven exploration and reliability-aware distillation
authors: Ruiqi Dong, Haotian Huang, Yubin Hu, Guixiang Zeng
abstract: Conventional two-stage distillation first establishes a teacher through teacher-driven configuration exploration, a costly first stage for complex materials, and then uses its predictions to supervise students, potentially propagating teacher-label errors. Here, we propose distillation-driven teacher-student co-evolution (DICE), which uses a fast student to accelerate configuration exploration and replaces the fixed teacher-to-student sequence with alternating student and teacher updates. A representation-based support-assessment algorithm routes high-support configurations to teacher labelling and selects low-support configurations for density functional theory (DFT) calculations to update the teacher, thereby reducing the risk of teacher-label error propagation to students. Across Al2O3 (structural ceramics), yttria-stabilised zirconia (solid electrolytes) and MIL-120(Al) (a metal-organic framework), DICE develops reliable compact potentials using only 140-494 target DFT reference configurations per system; total recorded student exploration times per system are just 2.6-5.1% of the corresponding teacher-driven estimates. Combining computational efficiency with broad applicability across diverse material systems, DICE provides a practical route to developing reliable compact interatomic potentials.

infographic.key_insight: DICE co-evolves fast student and teacher interatomic potentials, accelerating configuration exploration while limiting propagation of unreliable teacher labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a more efficient route to compact potentials for atomistic simulations of ceramics, solid electrolytes and metal–organic frameworks.
method: Use a fast student potential to explore configurations.
Assess representation-based support: route high-support configurations to teacher labelling and low-support configurations to DFT.
Alternate teacher and student updates rather than using fixed two-stage distillation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Al2O3, yttria-stabilised zirconia and MIL-120(Al), DICE used 140–494 target DFT reference configurations per system; recorded student exploration times were 2.6–5.1% of corresponding teacher-driven estimates.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability depends on support assessment correctly flagging configurations that need DFT; the reported timing comparison concerns exploration, not total workflow cost.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerating interatomic potential development through student-driven exploration and reliability-aware distillation

title: Prediction and characterisation of cation topology of pentanary high-entropy alloy (MoWNbTaV)S$_2$
authors: Shubham Agarwal, Tahir Wahab, Jesper Byggmästar, Antonio Cammarata, Tomas Polcar
abstract: High-entropy transition-metal dichalcogenides offer properties tuned by composition, yet two basic questions remain open: which arrangement of the metals forms under synthesis conditions, and how it can be recognised in experiment. Density functional theory (DFT) cannot sample the vast space of possible arrangements, and the ground-state energies usually employed to screen them do not take into account the temperatures at which these materials are made. This work solves both issues for the pentanary (MoWNbTaV)S\textsubscript{2} monolayer with a Gaussian approximation potential trained on DFT data by iterative learning. Gibbs free energy calculations reveal that vibrational entropy reshapes the stability ranking, while five selected configurations retain their trigonal-prismatic framework during nanosecond molecular dynamics up to \qty{1300}{\kelvin}. Raman and infrared spectra combine parent-monolayer signatures with disorder-activated modes, providing fingerprints for experimental identification. % The predicted lattice parameter follows Vegard's law and agrees within \qty{0.8}{\percent} with X{-}ray diffraction on a sputtered alloy film, which identifies the solid solution but not the arrangement of its metals: distinguishing between arrangements requires the vibrational fingerprints. The potential and its development workflow enable further atomistic simulations and offer a transferable approach to screening related two-dimensional high-entropy materials.

infographic.key_insight: Vibrational entropy changes the predicted stability ranking of cation arrangements in monolayer (MoWNbTaV)S₂, while vibrational spectra provide fingerprints for distinguishing them.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A DFT-trained machine-learning potential enables larger-scale screening of atomic arrangements in two-dimensional high-entropy materials.
method: Train a Gaussian approximation potential on DFT data through iterative learning.
Calculate Gibbs free energies and test thermal stability with molecular dynamics.
Predict Raman and infrared spectra to identify cation arrangements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Five selected configurations retained their trigonal-prismatic framework during nanosecond molecular dynamics at temperatures up to 1300 K.
infographic.watch_item: The predicted arrangements and spectral fingerprints require experimental validation; nanosecond stability does not establish long-term stability or synthesis outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Prediction and characterisation of cation topology of pentanary high-entropy alloy (MoWNbTaV)S$_2$

title: Interface-Engineered Piezoelectricity and Electromechanical Coupling in Two-Dimensional van der Waals Heterostructures
authors: Shivanand Yadav, Raihan Ahammed, Umer Ali, B. S. Bhadoria, Yogesh S. Chauhan, Amit Agarwal
abstract: Interfaces between dissimilar two-dimensional (2D) materials provide a route to engineer electromechanical responses that are not intrinsic to the individual constituent layers. Here, we use high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate 461 van der Waals heterostructures constructed from 57 2D monolayers and establish a materials-design framework linking work-function mismatch, interfacial charge redistribution, dipole formation, and strain-dependent electromechanical response. We find that heterostructure formation generates out-of-plane interfacial dipoles via charge redistribution between the constituent layers, while biaxial in-plane strain systematically modulates them. The resulting heterostructures exhibit two distinct regimes: metallic interfaces with strain-tunable interfacial dipoles and semiconducting heterostructures with well-defined piezoelectric responses. For the latter, Berry-phase (BP) calculations independently validate the charge-density-difference (CDD) approach, which is generally applicable to all representative systems, with piezoelectric coefficients calculated via two methods agreeing to within 10%. Among 24 selected heterostructures, effective biaxial interfacial electromechanical coefficients reach 83.35 pCm-1 . These results demonstrate that the interface can serve as the active element governing electromechanical coupling and provide a computationally guided strategy for designing strain-tunable out-of-plane electromechanical responses in 2D van der Waals heterostructures.

infographic.key_insight: Interfaces between dissimilar 2D layers create out-of-plane dipoles that can be tuned by in-plane strain, enabling interface-engineered electromechanical responses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Work-function mismatch and interfacial charge redistribution offer design handles for strain-tunable 2D electromechanical materials.
method: High-throughput DFT screening of 461 van der Waals heterostructures built from 57 monolayers.
Charge-density-difference analysis linking interfacial charge redistribution, dipoles, and biaxial strain.
Berry-phase validation of piezoelectric responses in semiconducting heterostructures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 24 selected heterostructures, effective biaxial interfacial electromechanical coefficients reach 83.35 pC/m; charge-density-difference and Berry-phase piezoelectric coefficients agree within 10% for semiconducting systems.
infographic.watch_item: The results are computational predictions; metallic-interface dipole tunability should not be conflated with well-defined semiconductor piezoelectricity.
infographic.paper_title: Interface-Engineered Piezoelectricity and Electromechanical Coupling in Two-Dimensional van der Waals Heterostructures

title: Generation and non-thermal annealing of dislocations and atomic-scale roughness by nonlinear surface acoustic waves
authors: Yuan Xu, Maxim V. Shugaev, Leonid V. Zhigilei
abstract: Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) are widely used to probe near-surface material properties and microstructure, but their potential to drive permanent structural modification remains largely unexplored. Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations reveal the mechanisms of defect generation and evolution induced by nonlinear Rayleigh waves in Pt. Strong crystallographic dependence of the nonlinear evolution is observed. SAWs on Pt(111) undergo rapid nonlinear sharpening and shock formation, with localized elastic energy and increasing near-surface stresses, whereas much weaker sharpening on Pt(001) allows dissipation to compete effectively with shock formation. For sufficiently strong SAWs on Pt(111), Shockley partial dislocations are emitted from the surface when the resolved shear stress approaches the theoretical shear strength. The highly localized and rapidly changing stress field at the shock front activates multiple slip systems and promotes crossslip and reactions between Shockley partials, producing complex dislocation structures with sessile stair-rod segments. Subsequent SAW interactions activate dislocation sources on slip systems where the stress is insufficient for homogeneous nucleation, leading, in one case, to sequential emission of Shockley partials and formation of a subsurface twinned domain. Repeated SAW passages progressively reduce dislocation density, demonstrating SAW-driven nonthermal annealing. Dislocation interactions with the free surface generate atomic-scale steps, terraces, and other under-coordinated configurations, providing a microscopic pathway for permanent surface modification that may contribute to the acoustically enhanced catalytic activity observed on Pt surfaces. These results establish nonlinear SAWs as drivers of nonthermal defect generation, restructuring, and annealing, opening opportunities for acoustic processing of near-surface microstructure.

infographic.key_insight: Nonlinear surface acoustic waves can generate dislocations, restructure surfaces, and drive nonthermal defect annealing in platinum.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Acoustic processing could enable control of near-surface defects and atomic-scale roughness, with potential relevance to platinum catalysis.
method: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of nonlinear Rayleigh waves in platinum.
Comparison of wave evolution on Pt(111) and Pt(001).
Tracking of dislocation reactions, surface restructuring, and repeated-wave annealing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show rapid shock formation on Pt(111), weaker sharpening on Pt(001), and progressive dislocation-density reduction with repeated wave passages.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation is needed to establish practical wave amplitudes and whether the simulated surface changes enhance catalytic activity.
infographic.paper_title: Generation and non-thermal annealing of dislocations and atomic-scale roughness by nonlinear surface acoustic waves

title: Covalent Welding of Two-Dimensional Molecular Sheets into Ultra-Stiff, Super-Tough Polymeric Networks
authors: Xiaoli Gong, Guohu Luo, Jiaxin Wu, Jiayu Chen, Zhengqiao Yin, Zhipeng Yan
abstract: Since the inception of macromolecular science, polymers have been constructed from zero-dimensional monomers, a paradigm that funnels all stress through discrete one-dimensional chains. Driven by conformational entropy, polymer chains inevitably coil in three-dimensional space, precluding effective stress transfer, thereby compromising the ultimate mechanical performance. Two-dimensional (2D) molecular sheets, with intrinsic in-plane rigidity, could in principle circumvent this constraint. Yet in existing assemblies, where stress transfers efficiently within each molecular sheet but poorly between them, their exceptional properties fail to translate to the macroscale. Here, we demonstrate a 2D highly oriented molecular network (2D HOMN), an ultra-stiff, super-tough polymeric material constructed by the solid-state covalent welding of assembled 2D polyaramid sheets with flexible linkers pre-grafted at their peripheries. Enabled by efficient intersheet load sharing and energy dissipation, the welded films rival the modulus and strength of Kevlar 29 fibers, reaching 69.8 and 3.9 GPa, with impact toughness up to an order of magnitude beyond Kevlar composites. This designed intersheet covalent connectivity further renders the 2D HOMN impermeable to gas molecules and ions, resilient to radiation and efficient in thermal transport. This work establishes 2D molecular motifs as heterogeneous monomeric building blocks and provides a general strategy for constructing multifunctional polymeric networks.

infographic.key_insight: Covalently welding aligned 2D polyaramid sheets creates a polymer network that combines high stiffness and strength with exceptional impact toughness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This architecture could enable lightweight protective and barrier materials by improving load transfer between molecular sheets.
method: Assemble highly oriented 2D polyaramid sheets.
Pre-graft flexible linkers at sheet peripheries.
Covalently weld sheets in the solid state to promote intersheet load sharing and energy dissipation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a modulus of 69.8 GPa and strength of 3.9 GPa, rivaling Kevlar 29 fibers, with impact toughness up to an order of magnitude beyond Kevlar composites.
infographic.watch_item: Scalable fabrication and reproducibility of sheet alignment and intersheet welding remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Covalent Welding of Two-Dimensional Molecular Sheets into Ultra-Stiff, Super-Tough Polymeric Networks

title: Translation Method Bounds for 3D Isotropic Conductivity--Shear Modulus and the Search for Attaining Microstructures
authors: Justin Tahmassebpur, Tomás Arias
abstract: We compute conductivity--shear-modulus cross-property bounds in three-dimensional isotropic two-phase composites using the translation method, and obtain the tightest bounds reported to date. To assess attainability, we perform unit-cell topology optimization on thousands of distinct initial structures and compare optimized designs to the isotropic bounds using an effective-medium approximation that models the macroscopic material as an isotropic assembly of randomly oriented grains. The best jointly performing designs are consistently bicontinuous, triply periodic minimal surface-like microstructures; however, a small but notable gap to the translation bound remains.

infographic.key_insight: Translation-method bounds sharpen the known conductivity–shear-modulus trade-off for 3D isotropic two-phase composites, while optimized microstructures remain slightly below the bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These bounds provide benchmarks for designing composites that combine electrical or thermal conduction with resistance to shear deformation.
method: Compute conductivity–shear-modulus cross-property bounds using the translation method.
Run unit-cell topology optimization from thousands of distinct initial structures.
Compare designs with isotropic bounds using an effective-medium model of randomly oriented grains.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across thousands of initial structures, the best jointly performing designs were consistently bicontinuous and triply periodic minimal surface-like, with a small remaining gap to the bounds.
infographic.watch_item: Attainability remains unresolved, and comparisons rely on an effective-medium approximation of macroscopic isotropy.
infographic.paper_title: Translation Method Bounds for 3D Isotropic Conductivity--Shear Modulus and the Search for Attaining Microstructures
